title: A single-pheromone model accounts for empirical patterns of ant colony foraging

abstract: We present a computational model showing that a single pheromone accounts for empirical patterns of ant colony foraging previously modeled using two pheromones. Our model demonstrates that the dynamics of pheromone deposition, evaporation, and ant behavioral responses to concentration gradients can produce the full range of observed foraging patterns with a simpler single-pheromone mechanism.

methods.name: Reanalysis of Dussutour et al. (2009) Pheidole megacephala Y-maze data
methods.description: Uses the published Y-maze branch-choice results (Experiments 1, 2 and 4) of Dussutour et al. as the empirical target; no new ant experiments were run.
methods.evidence: The values depicted as circle sizes were read off from Dussutour Fig. 2.

methods.name: One-pheromone model with exponential decay and power-law amplification
methods.description: Models a single attractant pheromone that decays exponentially and is perceived through a concave power-law sensory amplification minus a noise level.
methods.evidence: Proposed pheromone measurement function M is a power-law amplification of the raw pheromone level ph, subtracting a small base level noise factor, B.

methods.name: Branch preference as a product of two sigmoid functions
methods.description: Choice probability is modeled as a product of logistic terms for the difference between branches and the overall signal robustness.
methods.evidence: The product of these terms in Eq. (2) models that strong branch preference occurs under a conjunction of two factors

methods.name: Manual fitting and L-BFGS-B optimization in Python/SciPy
methods.description: Parameters were set by manual adjustment, then optimized with SciPy's bounded L-BFGS-B minimizing squared error against values read from the original figures.
methods.evidence: Optimization method used is l-BFGS-B (Limited-memory Broy­ den–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno method with Box constraints).

methods.name: Simulation of the dynamic-environment food-switching experiment
methods.description: Simulated Experiment 4 with differing per-ant deposit rates on food vs no-food branches and total traffic around 50 ants per minute.
methods.evidence: We conducted a simulation of Dussutour et al. Experiment 4, with ant preference following the model above

key_findings: The main reported observations of Dussutour et al. can be explained by a one-pheromone model.
A one-pheromone model accounts for equal initial E+F preference across conditions followed by divergence after about 15 minutes.
The one-pheromone model also accounts for preference flipping in the dynamic-environment experiment, and one optimized parameter set fits both figures reasonably.
The authors conclude that two pheromones are plausible but unnecessary, so the original study is not dispositive evidence for a two-pheromone model.
The model predicts that with food on both branches traffic equalizes without the oscillation predicted by the two-pheromone model.
key_findings_evidence: Here we show that the main reported experimental observations can be explained by a one-pheromone model.

Clearly, a one-pheromone model can very handily account for the observation that the initial frequency of ants choosing the E + F branch is the same in the E + F vs N and E + F vs experiments but these fre­ quencies diverge after 15 min.
Through numerical optimization, a single set of values can be found that reasonably fits both Dussutour et al. Fig. 2 and Fig. 10.
it is plausible, but unnec­ essary, to hypothesize that these ants employ two distinct pheromones in order to account for the two principal results of the Dussutour et al. study
Our model makes a different prediction, namely that traffic and pheromone deposition equalizes without oscillation.
